content: External comparisons of population data are essential for evaluating the adequacy of the population data used in calculating health indicators. These indicators serve as denominators in rate or proportion calculations and provide critical information on coverage. The Data Quality Review (DQR) methodology includes two main components: a desk review and a facility survey. The desk review examines the quality of reported aggregate data for recommended program indicators using standardized metrics. The facility survey has two parts: (1) a health facility data verification component, which compares data from source documents with data reported to district authorities, and (2) a system assessment (SA) tool that evaluates the reporting system's capacity to produce high-quality data, identifying the causes of data quality issues. The DQR is not a one-time activity. Instead, it involves a multi-faceted approach, including routine monthly reviews of data quality integrated into health management information systems (HMIS) or other reporting systems. These reviews are part of a feedback cycle to identify and correct errors promptly. Additionally, an annual assessment evaluates the quality of health facility data used for health sector planning and program monitoring. While it is recommended to select indicators from a core list, countries can adapt or expand the set of indicators based on their specific needs and resources. A toolkit has been developed to establish a common understanding of data quality and institutionalize regular data quality assessments at the country level. This toolkit includes guidelines, tools, and resources for conducting annual DQRs, which can also be adapted for routine or in-depth programmatic reviews. The toolkit comprises the DQR Framework and Metrics Document, a Technical Guide, data collection tools, an automated spreadsheet for data analysis (excluding data verification), and electronic data entry forms for tablets. This toolkit was scheduled for publication in 2015, with additional tools under development to enhance analysis. Efforts are also underway to integrate DQR metrics into the DHIS2 system, which will facilitate regular data quality assessments for countries using DHIS2 as their HMIS. In-depth data quality reviews, typically focusing on a single disease or program area, are conducted periodically (every three to five years) and contribute to program reviews. Strategic information is vital for decision-making at all levels of the health system. It supports program planning, prioritization, improvement, and accountability. At the service level, healthcare providers require information for managing patient care, monitoring service quality, and improving facility management. At the national and subnational levels, health program managers need reliable and timely data to assess program performance, guide corrective actions, and allocate resources effectively. Globally, ministries of health and international agencies use strategic information to monitor progress toward targets, inform policy, and allocate resources. Data analysis transforms raw data into actionable information by synthesizing health trends and identifying gaps in service delivery. Cascade analysis, for example, identifies points of attrition in the continuum of care, such as HIV testing, treatment initiation, and retention, to target interventions and improve outcomes. Program reviews are integral to the program cycle, enabling stakeholders to assess performance, identify challenges, and make evidence-based decisions. These reviews should be based on high-quality strategic information and assess the program's impact, outcomes, and inputs. The process involves three stages: desk analysis, field review, and overall analysis with recommendations. Desk analysis compiles available data on program achievements, while field reviews assess service delivery in real-time. The final stage synthesizes findings to inform future planning and policy development. Countries should take ownership of program reviews, aligning them with national program cycles and broader development efforts. Reviews should be conducted at different stages of the program cycle and tailored to specific needs, ensuring they contribute to improved program performance and health outcomes.
